stories.title: Charity wants bee, bird and butterfly population boost
summary: Berkshire, Buckinghamshire and Oxfordshire Wildlife Trust aims to raise £70,000 for the project.

stories.title: Hidden climate superpower: Why some ocean “snow” carries six times more carbon
summary: Scientists have discovered that the stickiness of underwater “marine snow” plays a surprisingly important role in how much carbon reaches the deep ocean.
Gooier particles resist bacterial breakdown and can transport more than six times as much carbon to the depths, revealing an unexpected connection between ocean slime and Earth's climate.

stories.title: A glimmer of good news for Britain's sleepy dormouse
summary: New figures suggest hazel dormice may be recovering after decades of decline, with warmer summers boosting survival.

stories.title: Scientists discover stunning new Amazon fish that may already be endangered
summary: Researchers have discovered a stunning new species of tiny orange-patterned fish in the Brazilian Amazon, but its survival may already be at risk.
Named Laimosemion laranja, the brilliantly colored killifish measures less than three centimeters long and was found in just three small forest pools.
Its extremely limited habitat is threatened by mining, deforestation, pollution, and expanding development.

stories.title: Scientists wipe out deadly brain tumors in every mouse tested with new cancer therapy
summary: Scientists at UC San Francisco have developed a powerful new cancer therapy that remains inactive until it reaches the brain, where it switches on to attack deadly tumors.

The engineered immune cells, called B-SYNC CAR-T cells, completely eliminated diffuse midline glioma (DMG), an aggressive childhood brain cancer that is almost always fatal within a year, in two mouse models.

stories.title: An ancient ocean full of giant predators reveals a surprising twist in evolution
summary: A remarkable fossil discovery in Colombia is challenging how scientists understand major evolutionary changes in Earth's history.

Researchers uncovered an incredibly diverse ancient marine ecosystem where giant reptiles, sharks, and other creatures thrived as older evolutionary groups approached extinction and newer ones emerged.
They call this previously unrecognized pattern a "Biotic Inflection," suggesting that major transformations in life can occur without mass extinctions.

stories.title: Einstein's equations reveal how gravity could break, reconnect, and release energy
summary: More than a century after Einstein revolutionized our understanding of gravity, scientists have uncovered a surprising new phenomenon hidden within his equations.

Researchers at Columbia University and Universidad Adolfo Ibáñez have identified a theoretical process called "gravitational reconnection," in which structures within gravitational fields can break apart and reconnect, transferring energy into matter.

stories.title: Dormice 'thrive' at National Trust site
summary: Killerton National Trust has 100 nest boxes across its estate in Devon.

stories.title: A nuclear blast could save Earth from an asteroid, but there's a catch
summary: A nuclear explosion might save Earth from a deadly asteroid, but new research suggests that hitting the wrong side could make the difference between success and disaster.
Scientists found that an asteroid's irregular shape can dramatically affect how it responds to an X-ray blast, with deflection effectiveness varying nearly fivefold depending on the angle.

stories.title: Ancient Siberian tomb reveals surprising secrets of cannabis use 2,800 years ago
summary: Scientists investigating a 2,800-year-old Siberian tomb discovered roughly 1,000 cannabis seeds and chemical evidence suggesting ancient Scythians used the plant for its intoxicating effects.
The remarkable find, surrounded by evidence of elaborate burial rituals and animal sacrifices, offers the oldest directly dated archaeological evidence of psychoactive cannabis use.

stories.title: Countryside managers prepare for climate change
summary: North Pennines National Landscape's plan includes restoring peatland and wildfire preparedness.

stories.title: Hundreds of seagrass shoots found in estuary
summary: There were fears a restoration trial may not succeed when only six seedlings had emerged in April.

stories.title: Scientists discover hidden brain changes linked to common sleep disorders
summary: Scientists have discovered that sleep disorders are associated with structural changes in brain regions that control attention, decision-making, and emotions, potentially explaining why disrupted sleep can affect everyday thinking and behavior.
The findings, drawn from 57 brain imaging studies, reveal both shared and disorder-specific patterns that could lead to more targeted treatments.

stories.title: Scientists squeeze record-breaking X-ray power into an incredibly tiny spot
summary: Scientists have created record-breaking X-ray flashes lasting just 300 attoseconds, concentrating enormous power into an incredibly tiny spot.
The breakthrough could unlock a new way to observe electrons in action and potentially control the ultrafast processes that drive chemical reactions.

stories.title: Stronger flu shot linked to nearly 55% lower Alzheimer's risk
summary: A surprising new study suggests that a stronger flu shot could offer older adults significantly greater protection against Alzheimer's disease.

stories.title: Mysterious gas leaks suggest Mars may still be volcanically alive
summary: Mysterious gas emissions and fresh volcanic fissures suggest that Mars may not be geologically dead after all, with hot magma potentially still active deep underground.
The discovery could point to hidden pockets of warmth and chemical energy capable of supporting microbial life beneath the Red Planet’s surface.

stories.title: A hidden limit of space and time could unlock electronics 100,000 times faster
summary: Scientists have discovered a surprising quantum limit that prevents electrons from being tracked with unlimited precision in both space and time.
The breakthrough could pave the way for manipulating chemical reactions and developing electronics hundreds of thousands of times faster than today's technology.
